headline: weak
texts: Several core areas need rebuilding, and that is a clear starting point. Work through the review cards in the order listed, beginning with the traps you fell into confidently. Do the mechanism and signs first, because later management and imaging build on them. Then retake the module.
Gap: 'most common' is not holding. Appendicitis is the commonest abdominal surgical emergency, including non-obstetric in pregnancy. Review the opening card before anything else.
Gap: age and obstructing cause are not yet linked. Lymphoid hyperplasia predominates in children, faecolith in adults. Redo the child-versus-adult card.

Gap: the causal chain is not yet reliable. Obstruction comes first; periumbilical visceral pain shifts to the right iliac fossa when the peritoneum is involved, and the end artery explains rapid gangrene. Review the pathophysiology cards.
Gap: symptom order is not yet a tool. Pain first, then vomiting, then fever; vomiting first argues against appendicitis. Review the symptom order card.

Gap: the signs and positions are mixed up. Psoas is hip extension with retrocaecal; obturator is internal rotation of the flexed hip with pelvic; Rovsing is left iliac fossa pressure. Start with the sign contrast card.
Gap: Alvarado is not secure. Two items score 2 (RIF tenderness, leucocytosis), the rest 1, total 10; 7 or more is likely. Rebuild it from the table and practise the arithmetic card.
Gap: the imaging ladder is not secure. Ultrasound first in children and pregnancy, MRI if inconclusive in pregnancy, CECT most accurate in adults. Review the imaging cards by patient group.

Gap: pregnancy testing and look-alikes are not yet automatic. Beta-hCG comes first in women of reproductive age; each group has mimics, such as mittelschmerz or caecal carcinoma. Review the differential card.

Gap: the choice between operating and antibiotics-first is not secure. Appendicectomy is the treatment of choice; antibiotics-first is for selected uncomplicated adults. Review the management qualifiers card.

Gap: mass, abscess and interval surgery are mixed up. A mass is conservative, an abscess drained under imaging, and older patients need colonoscopy or CT before selective interval surgery. Redo the management ladder cards.

Gap: the complication lists are merged. Disease: perforation, mass, abscess, pylephlebitis. Operation: wound infection, faecal fistula, stump appendicitis, ilioinguinal injury. Rebuild both lists and review the nerve card.
Gap: the tumour and its size rule are not yet held. Carcinoid is commonest; under 2 cm appendicectomy usually suffices, larger needs right hemicolectomy. Review the tumour card.

You swapped the psoas and obturator manoeuvres. You may have corrected this on the spot, but a retry at the same question does not show it has held. Psoas is pain on hip extension; obturator is pain on internal rotation of the flexed hip. Say the movement first, then the name. Next, meet it again on a fresh question: do the review card for this trap.

You tied a sign to the wrong appendix position. You may have corrected this on the spot, but a retry at the same question does not show it has held. Psoas goes with a retrocaecal appendix on the muscle; obturator and right rectal tenderness go with a pelvic appendix. Ask which organ the appendix touches. Next, meet it again on a fresh question: do the review card for this trap.

You ran Rovsing's sign backwards. You may have corrected this on the spot, but a retry at the same question does not show it has held. Rovsing's sign is pressure in the left iliac fossa causing pain in the right. Say it as 'press here, hurts there'. Next, meet it again on a fresh question: do the review card for this trap.

You reversed the pain pathway or the causal chain. You may have corrected this on the spot, but a retry at the same question does not show it has held. The chain starts with obstruction and rising pressure; early pain is periumbilical and shifts when the parietal peritoneum is inflamed. Say the steps in order. Next, meet it again on a fresh question: do the review card for this trap.

You put vomiting ahead of pain. You may have corrected this on the spot, but a retry at the same question does not show it has held. In appendicitis pain comes first, then vomiting, then fever; vomiting first argues against it. Next, meet it again on a fresh question: do the review card for this trap.

You misweighted the Alvarado score or read it as a diagnosis. You may have corrected this on the spot, but a retry at the same question does not show it has held. Only right iliac fossa tenderness and leucocytosis score 2, out of 10; 7 or more makes appendicitis likely, not certain. Next, meet it again on a fresh question: do the review card for this trap.

You treated a negative ultrasound as excluding appendicitis in an adult. You may have corrected this on the spot, but a retry at the same question does not show it has held. An unhelpful scan does not end the work-up; contrast-enhanced CT is the most accurate test in adults. Next, meet it again on a fresh question: do the review card for this trap.

You chose CT first for a child or pregnant patient. You may have corrected this on the spot, but a retry at the same question does not show it has held. Ultrasound is first in children and pregnancy; contrast CT is the most accurate test in adults. Check who the patient is. Next, meet it again on a fresh question: do the review card for this trap.

You put MRI first in pregnancy. You may have corrected this on the spot, but a retry at the same question does not show it has held. Graded-compression ultrasound is the first rung; MRI without gadolinium is the second, when ultrasound is inconclusive. Next, meet it again on a fresh question: do the review card for this trap.

You answered from the old ultrasound key for an adult. You may have corrected this on the spot, but a retry at the same question does not show it has held. Current practice is ultrasound first in children and pregnancy, and contrast-enhanced CT as the most accurate test in adults. Next, meet it again on a fresh question: do the review card for this trap.

You skipped or delayed the pregnancy test. You may have corrected this on the spot, but a retry at the same question does not show it has held. In any woman of reproductive age, beta-hCG comes before imaging or theatre, because ectopic pregnancy changes the plan. Next, meet it again on a fresh question: do the review card for this trap.

You picked a more dramatic condition as the most common. You may have corrected this on the spot, but a retry at the same question does not show it has held. Most common means most frequent: appendicitis is the commonest abdominal surgical emergency, and carcinoid the commonest appendix tumour. Next, meet it again on a fresh question: do the review card for this trap.

You assumed right iliac fossa pain always means appendicitis. You may have corrected this on the spot, but a retry at the same question does not show it has held. Each group has look-alikes, such as mesenteric lymphadenitis in children, mittelschmerz and PID in women, and caecal carcinoma in older patients. Next, meet it again on a fresh question: do the review card for this trap.

You ignored the age when naming the cause of the block. You may have corrected this on the spot, but a retry at the same question does not show it has held. Lymphoid hyperplasia predominates in children and young people; a faecolith in adults, as lymphoid tissue atrophies with age. Next, meet it again on a fresh question: do the review card for this trap.

You merged complications of the disease with those of the operation. You may have corrected this on the spot, but a retry at the same question does not show it has held. Pylephlebitis, mass and abscess come from the disease; wound infection, faecal fistula and stump appendicitis follow surgery. Next, meet it again on a fresh question: do the review card for this trap.

You named a neighbouring nerve instead of the one a gridiron incision endangers. You may have corrected this on the spot, but a retry at the same question does not show it has held. The ilioinguinal nerve is the one at risk, leading to a right inguinal hernia. Next, meet it again on a fresh question: do the review card for this trap.

You took 'treatment of choice' to mean the only treatment. You may have corrected this on the spot, but a retry at the same question does not show it has held. Appendicectomy is the treatment of choice, but antibiotics-first is accepted for selected CT-proven uncomplicated adults. Next, meet it again on a fresh question: do the review card for this trap.

You offered antibiotics-first without its conditions. You may have corrected this on the spot, but a retry at the same question does not show it has held. It suits selected adults with CT-proven uncomplicated disease and no appendicolith; an appendicolith predicts failure. Next, meet it again on a fresh question: do the review card for this trap.

You applied interval appendicectomy routinely after a mass. You may have corrected this on the spot, but a retry at the same question does not show it has held. It is now selective, and patients over about 40 need colonoscopy or CT to exclude caecal carcinoma. Next, meet it again on a fresh question: do the review card for this trap.

You went straight to surgery or open drainage. You may have corrected this on the spot, but a retry at the same question does not show it has held. A stable mass gets the Ochsner-Sherren regimen; a drainable abscess gets image-guided percutaneous drainage with antibiotics. Next, meet it again on a fresh question: do the review card for this trap.
You tend to pair items correctly in form but attach them to the wrong partner. Rebuild the pair from the anatomy it depends on rather than recalling the pair.
You tend to run a sequence or direction backwards, starting from the end picture. Narrate the process cause first, 'press here, hurts there' or 'blockage, then pressure'.
You tend to start with the favoured diagnosis and skip the step that comes first. Ask 'what first, and why' before committing to a plan.
You tend to treat the first or most accurate test as the whole pathway. Think in rungs: what comes first, what comes after an unhelpful result.
You tend to drop the qualifier, such as age, pregnancy or appendicolith, and apply a general answer. Circle the patient detail before looking at the options.
You tend to answer from a remembered past-paper key without checking current practice. In such stems, give the old key and the modern view as a pair.
You tend to read a qualifier or a pattern too narrowly: 'most common' as 'most serious', or a classic picture as the only one. Underline the qualifier, then ask what else fits.
You tapped Guessing on three or more answers you got right. Your knowledge is ahead of your confidence. Next time, give a one-line reason before answering, and tap Sure when you can.
You opened hints three or more times. Using them is fine early on; the aim is to need them less. Pick two objectives you hinted on and try the matching cards cold before your next session.

Review the cards in the order shown: confident errors first, then gaps, then shaky. Do two or three per sitting, answer before reading, then retake this module in about a week to see which models have changed.
